docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Compute Metaheuristic Engine for Python (cmenpy, pronounced /siːmɛnpaɪ/) is an extensible, vectorized Python framework for designing and prototyping metaheuristic and population-based optimization algorithms.

pip install cmenpy          # runtime: numpy only (pure-Python kernels)
pip install "cmenpy[numba]" # recommended: compiles kernels with Numba

An optimizer is a function — or a class — that steps a population forward one epoch at a time. This is a complete one:

import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def my_algorithm(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
        ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
    )
    for _ in epoch:
        pop.compute << np.clip(
            ~pop.extract + ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)),
            ctx.bounds.low,
            ctx.bounds.up,
        )


best_fitness, best_x = my_algorithm(x=1).solve(
    lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 3), epochs=150, pop_size=15
)

solve runs the model against any objective and returns the best solution found and its fitness.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Flat populations. Solutions live in one NumPy array — the fitness column and the vectors share a single buffer. No per-individual objects.
  • Two declaration styles. @cm.declare wraps a function that drives the run; @cm.template wraps a class with initialize/evolve. Both produce the same solve contract.
  • Reusable operator modules. @cm.module bundles kernels, helpers and cm.Constant fields that any number of models inherit.
  • Compiled kernels. @cm.precompile, @cm.vectorize and @cm.reduce defer Numba compilation to first use and cast by annotation.
  • Benchmark ready. Reference test functions plug in directly from the LTSIM companions opfunu-core and enoppy-core — see Test functions.

Start with the Quickstart, benchmark with Test functions, build your own optimizer with Build a custom model, or look things up in the API reference. See the Roadmap for what is coming in 2026b2.

docs.text:
cmenpy is deliberately an engine — it ships no benchmark suite. For reference test functions, use the LTSIM companions:

Library Import Domain Size opfunu-core import opfunu numerical benchmarks (classical + CEC 2005–2022) 500+ functions enoppy-core import enoppy real-world engineering problems (constrained) 50+ problems

Both are GPL v3, maintained forks of the original opfunu / enoppy libraries. Install them with cmenpy:

pip install "cmenpy[benchmarks]"
# or, in this repository:
uv sync --extra benchmarks

docs.title: Numerical benchmarks (opfunu-core)
docs.text:
Every opfunu function exposes evaluate(x) (one solution vector in, one fitness out) and bounds — a sequence of (low, up) pairs that cm.Bounds accepts directly. The two together plug into any model:

from opfunu.name_based import Ackley01

import cmenpy as cm


f = Ackley01(ndim=5)                # 5-D Ackley: global minimum 0 at origin

model = MyAlgorithm(seed=1)
best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
    f.evaluate, f.bounds, epochs=200, pop_size=30
)
  • Variable-dimension functions (Ackley01, Griewank, Alpine01, …) take an ndim keyword; fixed-dimension ones (Booth, Zirilli, …) validate the solution length at call time.
  • Discover functions with opfunu.FUNC_DATABASE (name-based), opfunu.CEC_DATABASE, or opfunu.get_functions_by_classname("Griewank").
  • CEC functions shift/rotate their landscapes, so their minimum is not at the origin — read the printed best value against the function's reported optimum, not against zero.

docs.title: Why scoring is row-by-row here
docs.text:
f.evaluate scores one solution per call, so an opfunu objective runs through the row-by-row path (scoring modes). For the vectorized fast path, write the block form of the function once — and combine it with the compiled kernel pattern:

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


def ackley_block(X):
    n = X.shape[1]
    s1 = np.sum(X**2, axis=1)
    s2 = np.sum(np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * X), axis=1)
    return -20.0 * np.exp(-0.2 * np.sqrt(s1 / n)) - np.exp(s2 / n) + 20.0 + np.e


model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(ackley_block), f.bounds, epochs=200, pop_size=30)

docs.title: Engineering problems (enoppy-core)
docs.text:
enoppy problems wrap objective and constraints into a penalized evaluation. Two integration details:

  • problem.evaluate(x) returns a one-element array, so coerce to float;
  • bounds arrive as per-dimension lb / ub arrays; zip them for cm.Bounds.
import numpy as np
from enoppy.paper_based.pdo_2022 import ThreeBarTrussProblem

import cmenpy as cm


prob = ThreeBarTrussProblem()


def objective(x):
    return float(np.asarray(prob.evaluate(x)).item())


bounds = cm.Bounds(list(zip(prob.lb, prob.ub)))

model = MyAlgorithm(seed=1)
best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(objective, bounds, epochs=300, pop_size=40)
  • prob.get_objs(x) / prob.get_cons(x) expose the raw objective and constraint values if you want your own penalty (prob = ThreeBarTrussProblem(f_penalty=...)).
  • Native constraint handling is planned (roadmap: constraint handling in the backlog); for now evaluate's penalty is the supported contract.

The runnable version of this snippet is example/engineering_demo.py.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Numba is now an optional backend. The core install only requires NumPy;
  • The numba compile option controls whether compilation takes place:
  • Uncompiled kernels keep their specs (arguments are still auto-cast) and run
  • cm.prepare(model) reports uncompiled kernels as ["<python>"].
  • Models accept a prepare constructor option: `MyOptimizer(numba=True,
  • Kernels cast array-protocol arguments **automatically, even when declared

  • from cmenpy import prange binds numba's prange when the backend is

  • Composable termination criteria in cmenpy.terminator: MaxEvaluation (with cm.Terminator(nfe=...) as an alias), MaxEpoch, MaxPatience, MaxTime, EpochStagnation, TargetFitness, SpreadFitness and UserInterrupt, combined with & (AND) and | (OR) — issue #33.

  • Opt-in run history in cmenpy.history: in-memory, JSONL, CSV and NPZ sinks with summary and full-snapshot levels, retention options, and a schema-versioned reader — issue #35.
  • Domain decoders and heterogeneous search spaces in cmenpy.decoder and cmenpy.space (floats, integers, strings, categories, sequences, binaries, booleans) with both the cm.Space[...] standard form and the cm.Space(float=..., string=...) sugar form — issue #34.
  • Multiobjective optimization: vector fitness columns, per-objective sense, Pareto dominance utilities, fronts and crowding distance, and an NSGA-II example — issue #36.
  • Per-dimension search-space helpers: Bounds.lows, Bounds.ups, Bounds.sample() and Bounds.clip() — issue #37.
  • Benchmark companions: reference test functions from opfunu-core (500+ numerical functions) and engineering problems from enoppy-core are now used across the examples, the test suite and the new Test functions guide page; install them with the new benchmarks extra — issue #39.
  • example/engineering_demo.py: a constrained engineering problem solved with enoppy-core.
  • Roadmap documentation page.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The changelog has a single source of truth (CHANGELOG.md); the docs site includes it via a snippet instead of keeping a second copy that can drift.
  • Every optimizer example solves an opfunu-core benchmark function instead of an inline hand-rolled objective.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The population agent types (BaseAgent, ImmutableAgent, MutableAgent) and the AgentTemplate protocol. Read an individual through the array-first surface — pop.access[pop.best] (or pop.X / pop.F) for the solution and fitness — and re-score a row with pop.compute[pop.best] << solution, which writes the row and charges one evaluation, the same path the old MutableAgent.solution setter took.
  • Unused surface around that array-first path: TargetFunction.apply_axis() (the buffer already does the same row-wise scoring inline) and TargetFunction.f (an alias of evaluate); KernelMask.passive; StreamOperator.rows and StreamOperator.columns; DefaultGenerator.seed; the SpecType typing alias (it was just typing.Any); and the __operator_module__ marker attribute, which nothing read — @cm.module still keeps the class identity and installs its constants.
  • Positional field values on cm.declare: it was accepted and ignored, so @cm.declare(...) is now written @cm.declare(). Declare fields with keyword arguments, as before.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The NFE counter now charges one evaluation per individual scored for every way pop.compute selects rows. A NumPy row index — what pop.best, pop.worst and pop.sort return — used to be treated as a block: it spent ndim evaluations and then called the objective with a single solution, which raised for vectorized targets. pop.insert, MutableAgent.solution writes and the documented pop.compute[pop.best] << solution recipe are affected by the same dispatch and are fixed by it.
  • Row-wise scoring no longer raises when a mask selects nothing (an emptied roster, or no row passing cm.is_best); such a selection now spends zero evaluations instead of failing inside np.apply_along_axis.
  • pop.compute also accepts index iterators (pop.compute[~pop]) and the buffer's KernelMask (pop.compute[ctx.buff.mask]) as selectors.
  • TargetFunction.evaluate_matrix rejects a bare solution vector with a clear message instead of spending ndim evaluations on it; a single solution is scored with TargetFunction.evaluate, which now dispatches a vectorized target as a one-row block.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• cm.cast(value, dtype=None, layout="A") is the explicit way to turn a

  • @cm.module turns a class into a reusable Operator Module (a Ruby-style mixin). It marks the class, materializes its cm.Constant annotations and keeps it usable as a plain base: @cm.template class GA(Selection) inherits kernels, helper methods and fields from Selection. Name collisions resolve through the MRO, and cm.prepare(model) now reports kernels inherited from an Operator Module (compilation walks cls.__mro__ instead of vars(cls)).

  • cm.Constant[type, value] declares a fixed, read-only field for @cm.template models and @cm.module Operator Modules. The value is checked at declaration, exposed through the class as a read-only descriptor (self.name / Cls.name), and is never constructor-bound — passing it to the model call raises TypeError. Constants flow into every implementing model via normal inheritance, so they work identically on a template and on an Operator Module.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Numba decorators accept parameter annotations ("Array[float, 2]", "Scalar[float]", and mypy-clean Annotated[..., cm.Array[...]]), in addition to the positional cm.Array / cm.Scalar markers.

docs.title: Function style: @cm.declare
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def my_algorithm(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
        ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
    )
    for _ in epoch:  # one epoch of your operator, per iteration

docs.title: Class style: @cm.template
docs.text:
@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    a: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100)]

    w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        # ... generation `e` ...
        ...


model = MyAlgorithm(a=3, seed=1)
best = model.solve(lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 3), 150, 15)

Full version: example/hello_world_v2.py.

docs.title: The solve contract
docs.text:
(best_fitness, best_x) = model.solve(
    f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min"
)
  • f is a callable x -> float over one solution vector (or a vectorized target).
  • bounds is a cm.Bounds (e.g. cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * ndim)) — a reference benchmark's f.bounds satisfies the same contract (Test functions).
  • sense is "min" (default) or "max".

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
This document tracks the direction of cmenpy: what is in the next release, what is planned, and what is deliberately not going to be built here.

Status legend:

Status Meaning done shipped in a release in progress under development on the current milestone planned agreed scope, not started backlog desirable, not scheduled

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Vector first. The hot paths stay flat NumPy/Numba arrays; object wrappers are an interface, never the storage.
  • Non-monolithic. No plotting, no forced logging, no heavyweight dependencies. Persistence and reporting are opt-in adapters (history=..., terminator=...) that never run unless asked for.
  • Two declaration styles, one contract. @cm.declare and @cm.template keep producing the same solve(...) surface; new features extend both or neither, never only one.
  • Backward compatibility inside a channel. Additive changes ship freely; renames keep a deprecated alias for one release (see cm.jit → cm.precompile).

docs.title: 2026b2 — the next release
docs.text:
One active milestone that bundles the work of feature request #23 (split into #33 and #34) with the run-control and analysis features requested alongside it.

Issue Deliverable Status #33 Composable terminators (cmenpy.terminator) planned #34 Decoders and Space (cmenpy.decoder, cmenpy.space) planned #35 Run history, RAM + disk (cmenpy.history) planned #36 Multiobjective Pareto core planned #37 Per-dimension bounds (Bounds.lows/ups/sample/clip) planned #38 Changelog restructure + this roadmap in progress #39 Test functions: examples, docs and tests use opfunu-core / enoppy-core in progress

docs.title: Terminators (#33)
docs.text:
Stopping criteria become composable objects instead of hardcoded loop exits:

terminator = (
    cm.MaxEvaluation(nfe=50_000) & cm.MaxEpoch(limit=10_000)
) | cm.MaxPatience(ms=60_000)

model.solve(f, bounds, epochs=10_000, pop_size=40, terminator=terminator)

Python cannot overload && / ||, so & and | are the supported spelling. MaxPatience(ms=...) stops after N milliseconds without improvement and MaxTime(seconds=...) is the hard wall-clock cap. cm.Terminator(nfe=...) is kept as an alias of MaxEvaluation. Termination reasons surface in model.report.

docs.title: Decoders and Space (#34)
docs.text:
The decision space stays a flat continuous vector, but each slice of it can now be interpreted as a different domain type — integers, strings, categories, permutations, binaries — through BaseDecoder subclasses.

space = cm.Space[
    cm.floats(low=0.0, up=1.0),
    cm.integers(low=0, up=10),
    cm.strings("A", "B", "C"),
]

# sugar form (a call, since Space[float=...] is not valid Python syntax)
space = cm.Space(float=(0.0, 1.0), string=("a", "b", "c"))

solve(space=...) is additive; bounds= keeps working, and ctx.space exposes the decoder pipeline that runs immediately before fitness evaluation.

docs.title: Run history (#35)
docs.text:
Per-epoch records become storable in RAM or on disk, opt-in per run:

model.solve(..., history=True)             # in-memory summary
model.solve(..., history="run.jsonl")      # streamed summary
model.solve(..., history=cm.history.NPZ("run.npz", snapshots=True))

debug=True keeps its current full in-RAM behavior. A versioned reader (cm.history.load) returns the records without imposing pandas.

docs.title: Multiobjective core (#36)
docs.text: Vector-valued objectives end-to-end: per-objective sense, fitness stored as (pop, m) in the buffer, dominance/non-dominated sort/crowding in cmenpy.multiobjective, Pareto fronts on the population (pop.front, pop.crowding) and an NSGA-II reference example. Scalar runs keep their exact shapes and performance.

docs.title: Per-dimension bounds (#37)
docs.text: Bounds.low / Bounds.up expose only the first dimension, so the common rng.uniform(bounds.low, bounds.up, ...) idiom silently ignores unequal intervals. Bounds.lows, Bounds.ups, Bounds.sample() and Bounds.clip() fix this without breaking the existing accessors; examples and docs migrate to the new helpers.

docs.title: Test functions (#39)
docs.text: The engine ships without a benchmark suite — reference test functions come from the LTSIM companions opfunu-core (500+ numerical functions: classical name-based plus every CEC competition) and enoppy-core (50+ constrained engineering problems). Every example solves an opfunu function, example/engineering_demo.py shows enoppy, and tests/test_benchmarks.py keeps both integrations honest. See the Test functions guide.

docs.title: Backlog (not scheduled)
docs.text:
• Checkpoint / resume: serialize buffer, mask, RNG state and epoch so a run can continue from disk.
  • MOO quality indicators: hypervolume, IGD, front spread.
  • Constraint handling (penalty / feasibility rules) on top of decoders.
  • Batched and parallel target evaluation.
  • A reproducible benchmark suite (CEC-style functions).
  • Polished UserInterrupt signal handling.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text: cmenpy will stay a design and prototyping engine. We will not add: plotting or visualization, rigid logging frameworks, a model zoo of named algorithms as a core dependency, or non-GPU/non-NumPy numeric backends. Those belong in companion packages.

docs.title: Proposing work
docs.text: Open an issue first — see CONTRIBUTING.md. Ideas that are adopted land in the 2026b2 table above or in the backlog, and the changelog's Unreleased section is where they become visible.

docs.title: Build a custom model
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through implementing a custom optimizer from scratch with the @cm.template class style. We will build a (μ + λ) Evolution Strategy (Es): keep a parent population of size μ, produce λ offspring by Gaussian mutation each epoch, and select the best μ from the union of parents and offspring (elitist selection).

Along the way you will use every core piece of cmenpy: fields, the ctx object, the Population DSL, the comparators, and a compiled numba kernel.

Prerequisites

Comfortable with NumPy. You should have skimmed the Quickstart and Models overview.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]   # mutation step (initial)

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None: ...
    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None: ...

model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)
best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
    lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
)

Let's build it step by step.

docs.title: Step 1 — Declare the class and fields
docs.text:
Start with the skeleton. Class annotations declare tunable parameters with cm.Argument[type, (min, max), default] and free state with cm.Variable[type]:

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]

    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]
  • sigma is a tunable argument: range-checked, with a default, and settable at construction (EvolutionStrategy(sigma=0.1)).
  • offspring is a variable: internal state with no range or default. We will store the current generation's offspring here so evolve can both produce and score them.

A @cm.template model must implement two methods: initialize(self, ctx) (runs once) and evolve(self, e, ctx) (runs once per epoch). Let's add them next.

docs.title: Step 2 — Seed the population in initialize
docs.text:
initialize runs before any epoch. Build a PopulationSwarm over the buffer and write an initial random population with pop.compute << ..., which both inserts and scores the solutions:

def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
        ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
    )
  • ctx.buff is the flat buffer backing the population.
  • ctx.bounds.low / ctx.bounds.up are the box bounds — convenient for vectorized sampling.
  • pop.size is the number of active individuals.

After this line the whole parent population is randomly placed and evaluated.

docs.title: Step 3 — Produce offspring in evolve
docs.text:
evolve(self, e, ctx) is called once per epoch with the epoch index e. We mutate μ randomly chosen parents λ times. First, grab the active parent solutions (~pop.extract), then sample parent indices and perturb:

def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    parents = ~pop.extract                       # (μ, ndim) active solutions

    # Anneal the step size linearly over the run.
    self.offspring = self.sigma * (1.0 - e / ctx.epochs)

    idx = ctx.rng.integers(0, pop.size, pop.size)  # λ = μ
    kids = parents[idx]                            # pick parents at random

    noise = ctx.rng.standard_normal(kids.shape)
    mutated = np.clip(
        kids + self.offspring * noise,
        ctx.bounds.low,
        ctx.bounds.up,
    )

We reuse the buffer's snapshot to score the offspring in isolation, without clobbering the parents yet:

    n_pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff.snapshot)
    n_pop.compute << mutated

ctx.buff.snapshot

snapshot returns a fresh, empty buffer of the same shape wired to the same objective and sense. It is the idiomatic place to evaluate a candidate generation before merging it back.

docs.title: Step 4 — Elitist selection with cm.is_best
docs.text:
Now merge: keep, for each row, whichever of {parent, offspring} is better. The cm.is_best((new_F, old_F), ctx.sense) comparator returns the row indices where new beats old, respecting the optimization direction:

    mask = cm.is_best((n_pop.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
    pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask]
  • n_pop.F / pop.F are the fitness columns of the offspring and parents.
  • pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask] copies the winning offspring rows over their parents (access reads whole rows, assign writes them).

Because we never introduce a worse individual, the best solution is monotonically non-worsening — classic elitism. Note we used ctx.sense rather than a hard-coded comparison, so this model works for "min" and "max" alike.

docs.title: Step 5 — Compile the mutation with a numba kernel
docs.text:
The mutation loop above is plain NumPy. To make it run at numba speed, move the per-gene math into a @cm.precompile kernel declared as a method. Annotate the parameters so cmenpy knows how to cast and type them:

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]
    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

    @cm.precompile
    def mutate(
        K: "Array[float, 2]",
        N: "Array[float, 2]",
        s: "Scalar[float]",
        lo: "Scalar[float]",
        hi: "Scalar[float]",
    ):
        out = np.empty_like(K)
        for i in range(K.shape[0]):
            for j in range(K.shape[1]):
                v = K[i, j] + s * N[i, j]
                out[i, j] = min(max(v, lo), hi)   # clip to bounds
        return out

Then call it from evolve instead of the inline NumPy:

    mutated = self.mutate(kids, noise, self.offspring,
                          ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up)

Because mutate is a method on a @cm.template class, it participates in the model's compile options — you can force parallel, fastmath or cache at construction (see Compilation options). The kernel compiles lazily on first use; call model.prepare() to compile eagerly and inspect the signatures.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run it
docs.text:
Wire it all together and solve:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)

    def sphere(x):
        return float(np.sum(x**2))

    best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
        sphere, cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
    )
    print("best fitness:", best_fitness)
    print("best solution:", best_x)

solve returns (best_fitness, best_x). Pass debug=True to populate model.tracker with per-epoch history (EpochHistory records), and sense="max" to switch to maximization.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    """A (mu + lambda) Evolution Strategy with elitist selection."""

    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]

    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

    @cm.precompile
    def mutate(
        K: "Array[float, 2]",
        N: "Array[float, 2]",
        s: "Scalar[float]",
        lo: "Scalar[float]",
        hi: "Scalar[float]",
    ):
        out = np.empty_like(K)
        for i in range(K.shape[0]):
            for j in range(K.shape[1]):
                v = K[i, j] + s * N[i, j]
                out[i, j] = min(max(v, lo), hi)
        return out

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
            ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
        )

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        parents = ~pop.extract

        self.offspring = self.sigma * (1.0 - e / ctx.epochs)

        idx = ctx.rng.integers(0, pop.size, pop.size)
        kids = parents[idx]
        noise = ctx.rng.standard_normal(kids.shape)

        mutated = self.mutate(
            kids, noise, self.offspring, ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up
        )

        n_pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff.snapshot)
        n_pop.compute << mutated

        mask = cm.is_best((n_pop.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
        pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)

    def sphere(x):
        return float(np.sum(x**2))

    best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
        sphere, cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
    )
    print("best fitness:", best_fitness)
    print("best solution:", best_x)

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
Declare a tunable, range-checked model field.

Argument is a subscript-only marker that builds a typing.Annotated type understood by @cm.declare / @cm.template. It is never instantiated — only subscripted on a class annotation. Supported forms::

Argument[type]                  # required, no range/default
Argument[type, default]         # with a default value
Argument[type, (min, max)]      # range-checked, required
Argument[type, (min, max), default]

The subscript accepts target_type (the field's type), optionally a (min_val, max_val) range, and optionally a default_val. An unsupported form raises TypeError.

docs.title: Constant
docs.text:
Declare a fixed, read-only field for templates and operator mixins.

Constant is a subscript-only marker that builds a typing.Annotated type understood by @cm.template and @cm.module. The declared value is installed as a class-level descriptor, so it is visible as self.name/Cls.name but is never a constructor parameter::

Constant[type, value]    # a fixed value checked once at declaration

Constants work the same way on a @cm.template model and on a @cm.module mixin, where every implementing model inherits them.

docs.title: Variable
docs.text:
Declare a free internal-state field (no range check, no default).

Variable is a subscript-only marker for model state that is not a tunable parameter::

w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

It wraps target_type (the field's declared type) in typing.Annotated metadata marking it as delayed-init state.

apply(x: NDArrayType, idx: RowSelection | None = None) -> None

Vectorizes the target function to evaluate and update the solutions matrix.

The internal buffer stores "fitness" in column 0 and "solutions" or "x" from column 1 onwards. Supports updating a single row, a slice, a list/array of indices, a boolean mask, or the entire active matrix if idx is None.

docs.title: module
docs.text:
module(cls: type[_ModuleT]) -> type[_ModuleT]

Mark cls as a reusable Operator Module that models can mix in.

A class decorated with @cm.module behaves like a Ruby module: it groups metaheuristic operators — cm.precompile / cm.vectorize / cm.reduce kernels, plain helper methods and cm.Argument / cm.Variable / cm.Constant fields — so several @cm.template models can inherit the same behavior. Note that @cm.module returns a class, not a Python module.

The decorator keeps the class identity and materializes its cm.Constant annotations, so a constant is reachable (MyOps.P) even before any model includes the mixin. Mixin application is ordinary inheritance; name collisions resolve through the normal MRO, with the leftmost base winning.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cls type[_ModuleT]

The Operator Module class to mark.

required

Returns:

Type Description type[_ModuleT]

The same class, with its cm.Constant fields materialized.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If cls is not a class (for example a @cm.template model instance, which is not reusable as a mixin).

Examples:

::

@cm.module
class Selection:
    pressure: cm.Constant[float, 1.5]

    @cm.vectorize
    def clamp(x: cm.Array, lo: cm.Scalar, hi: cm.Scalar):
        return min(max(x, lo), hi)

@cm.template
class GA(Selection):
    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        ...  # can use self.pressure and self.clamp(...)

Declare target as able to evaluate a whole (pop, ndim) block.

The wrapped callable receives a 2-D array and must return one value per row, so np.sum(x**2, axis=1) replaces a per-row comprehension. The result is identical to the row-by-row evaluation, only dispatched once.

Examples:

model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere), bounds, 100, 40)

declare_from_class(cls: type[ModelProtocol]) -> TemplateOptimizerModel

Wrap cls in a TemplateOptimizerModel with a dynamic __init__.

The generated __init__ extracts the compile options (numba/ parallel/fastmath/cache), reads the class type hints (Annotated metadata carries ranges and defaults), validates the arguments and stores them as instance attributes before delegating to the original __init__.

numba controls whether the class kernels are compiled: False runs them as pure Python/NumPy, True demands compilation (ImportError without numba), and leaving it out compiles when numba is available. prepare forces compilation at construction: prepare=True compiles (or reports) every kernel during __init__ — the equivalent of calling model.prepare() immediately — while prepare=False (the default) keeps compilation lazy.

cm.Constant fields are materialized as read-only class descriptors by install_constants and skipped by the generated __init__: they are never constructor-bound, so passing one raises TypeError.

docs.title: Numba kernels
docs.text:
cmenpy wraps three Numba compiler paths — njit, vectorize and guvectorize — in decorators that add three things Numba does not give you on its own:

  1. Spec-driven casting. Declared specs (cm.Array, cm.Scalar) coerce every argument to the declared dtype/layout before the compiled code sees it, so plain Python lists and misaligned arrays just work.
  2. Deferred compilation. Each decorator returns a _Kernel descriptor that compiles on first use (or eagerly, when the signature is fully typed), so a model can inject its compile options before anything is compiled.
  3. Model-level compile options. A @cm.template model can set parallel/fastmath/cache once at instantiation and every kernel it inherits — including ones mixed in from an Operator Module — picks them up.

nopython=True is always enabled.

docs.title: The three families
docs.text:
Decorator Compiles to Kernel shape Typical use @cm.precompile numba.njit any function: loops, branches, whole blocks mutation, selection, block objectives @cm.vectorize numba.vectorize (ufunc) one scalar in, one scalar out elementwise helpers: clip, scale, activation @cm.reduce numba.guvectorize (gufunc) loop over core dimensions, output allocated row/matrix kernels: row clip, matmul, outer

Choosing one:

  • Loop over rows or a whole block yourself → @cm.precompile.
  • One element at a time, no loops → @cm.vectorize.
  • Loop over named core dimensions, with the output allocated for you → @cm.reduce.

cm.jit still exists as a deprecated alias of @cm.precompile and emits a DeprecationWarning.

docs.title: Where kernels live
docs.text:
A kernel can be declared in three places, and the difference matters only for compile options:

# 1. Module level — compiles with the decorator's own options.
@cm.precompile
def score(X: "Array[float, 2]"): ...

# 2. A @cm.template method — picks up the model's compile options.
@cm.template
class MyModel:
    @cm.precompile(parallel=True)
    def mutate(self, K: "Array[float, 2]"): ...

# 3. A @cm.module mixin — same as (2), through inheritance.

Only styles 2 and 3 receive a model's parallel/fastmath/cache flags; a module-level kernel uses the options you passed to the decorator and nothing else. See Compilation options for the exact precedence.

docs.title: Compilation lifecycle
docs.text:
Each decorator returns a _Kernel descriptor rather than a compiled function:

  • Fully typed signature (dtype and rank declared, or a raw numba signature string) → compilation happens at decoration time.
  • Partially typed or bare (e.g. just cm.Array) → the descriptor stays lazy and compiles on first call, when numba infers the concrete types.
  • Every distinct resolved option set (fastmath, cache, parallel, …) compiles once and is cached; switching a model's flags compiles a second variant rather than recompiling from scratch.

To force compilation before the hot loop, in order of preference:

model = MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True)
model.prepare()              # report {kernel: [signatures]} after compiling
cm.prepare(model)            # same, works for a model instance or a class
model.solve(f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, prepare=True)   # compile inside solve

docs.title: API
docs.text: Autodoc for the decorators, markers and introspection helpers lives in the API Reference → Functions.

docs.title: Compilation options
docs.text: Two places can set compile options: the decorator (@cm.precompile(parallel=True)) and, for a @cm.template model, the instantiation (MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True)). This page documents how the two merge, when a kernel sees which, and how to force and inspect compilation.

docs.title: The model options
Merging rules
docs.text:
The decorator's options are the base; the model's config upgrades them:

  • fastmath — enabled if either the model or the decorator asks for it.
  • cache — same: model or decorator enables it.
  • parallel, @cm.precompile (njit) — the kernel must opt in and the model must allow it. A kernel declared without parallel=True never compiles parallel, even when the model sets it.
  • parallel, @cm.vectorize / @cm.reduce (ufuncs) — enabled if either the model or the decorator asks for it. Ufuncs are parallel-safe by default, so the model can switch them on wholesale.
  • nopython=True is forced for the ufunc decorators regardless of any other setting.

docs.title: parallel precedence
docs.text:
Kernel opt-in Model parallel @cm.precompile result @cm.vectorize / @cm.reduce result True True parallel=True target="parallel" True not set parallel=True¹ target="parallel" not set True serial target="parallel" not set not set serial serial

¹ When the kernel is used standalone (module level, or accessed on the class) there is no model config, so the decorator flag alone decides.

docs.title: Where the model config applies
docs.text:
A _Kernel is a descriptor. Compilation resolves options at first use:

model = MyModel(seed=1, fastmath=True)
model.mutate(...)        # instance access → sees fastmath=True
MyModel.mutate           # class access → decorator options only
  • Instance access (self.kernel(...), model.kernel(...)) passes the model's _compile_options.
  • Class access (MyModel.kernel) and module-level kernels compile with the decorator's options only.

The same kernel compiled under two different configs exists side by side: the descriptor keeps one compiled function per distinct resolved option set, keyed by the merged options. Switching a model's flags therefore compiles a second variant rather than recompiling the first.

docs.title: Eager vs lazy
docs.text:
Signature state When it compiles fully typed (dtype and rank, or a raw numba signature string) at decoration time partially typed / bare on first call

Since options are only known at instantiation, model flags can never change whether a signature is eager — only with which options the (re)compilation happens.

docs.title: Forcing compilation
docs.text:
Compilation costs time on the first call. Warm up before timing or before a long run:

model = MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True, cache=True)

model.prepare()                       # -> {"mutate": ["none(...)"], ...}
cm.prepare(model)                     # same, model instance or class
model.solve(f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, prepare=True)   # compile inside solve

prepare() returns a {kernel_name: [signatures]} mapping and resolves kernels through the MRO, so an inherited Operator Module kernel is reported too.

docs.title: Inspecting a kernel
docs.text:
kernel = model.mutate                  # resolves + compiles for this model
kernel.signatures()                    # ["none(Array(float64, 2, C), ...)"]
kernel.targetoptions                   # the merged numba options dict

model.compile_options shows what the model will contribute; see the API Reference → Functions for the full surface.

docs.title: @cm.precompile (njit)
docs.text:
@cm.precompile maps to numba.njit. It is the general-purpose kernel: any function body — loops, branches, whole-block math — compiled with nopython always on.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.precompile
def square(X: "Array[float, 2]"):
    return X**2

docs.title: Calling forms
docs.text:
All of these are accepted; combine freely.

# Bare — lazy, inference at first call.
@cm.precompile
def f(X): ...

# Options.
@cm.precompile(parallel=True, fastmath=True)
def f(X): ...

# Positional specs (win over annotations).
@cm.precompile(cm.Array[float, 2], cm.Scalar[float])
def f(X, a): ...

# Annotations.
@cm.precompile
def f(X: "Array[float, 2]", a: "Scalar[float]"): ...

# Raw numba signature string.
@cm.precompile("float64(float64)")
def f(x): ...

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Effect fastmath=True Numba fastmath — faster, less precise FP parallel=True Numba parallel; the body must use nb.prange any other kwarg forwarded to njit verbatim (cache=True, boundscheck=False, nogil=True, inline="always", …) 
import numba as nb
import numpy as np


@cm.precompile(cm.Array, cm.Scalar, parallel=True)
def scale_rows(A, factor):
    out = np.empty_like(A)

    for i in nb.prange(A.shape[0]):     # prange is required for parallel
        out[i] = A[i] * factor

    return out

parallel needs prange

parallel=True only parallelizes numba.prange loops. A kernel with no prange compiles fine but runs serially — see Troubleshooting.

For a model method, parallel has a second gate: the kernel must opt in and the model must enable it (see Compilation options). At module level only the decorator flag matters.

docs.title: Return conventions
docs.text:
• Return a new array (np.empty, np.empty_like) or a scalar.
  • In-place kernels that write into a passed out array work too, as long as the layout matches the spec.
  • The returned dtype is whatever the body computes; declare specs if you need a specific one.

docs.title: Whole-block objective
docs.text:
The pattern from Target functions: score a whole (pop, ndim) block in one call.

@cm.precompile
def sphere_block(X: "Array[float, 2]"):
    out = np.empty(X.shape[0])

    for i in range(X.shape[0]):
        acc = 0.0
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            acc += X[i, j] * X[i, j]
        out[i] = acc

    return out

docs.title: Mutation with clipping
docs.text:
The kernel from Build a custom model: mutate a block of offspring and clip to bounds, with scalars cast from ctx.bounds.

@cm.precompile
def mutate(K: "Array[float, 2]", N: "Array[float, 2]",
           s: "Scalar[float]", lo: "Scalar[float]", hi: "Scalar[float]"):
    out = np.empty_like(K)

    for i in range(K.shape[0]):
        for j in range(K.shape[1]):
            v = K[i, j] + s * N[i, j]
            out[i, j] = min(max(v, lo), hi)

    return out

docs.title: Pairwise distances
docs.text:
A row-per-thread reduction, the classic prange case.

import numba as nb
import numpy as np


@cm.precompile(parallel=True)
def distances(X: "Array[float, 2]", Y: "Array[float, 2]"):
    D = np.empty((X.shape[0], Y.shape[0]))

    for i in nb.prange(X.shape[0]):
        for j in range(Y.shape[0]):
            acc = 0.0
            for k in range(X.shape[1]):
                d = X[i, k] - Y[j, k]
                acc += d * d
            D[i, j] = np.sqrt(acc)

    return D

docs.title: Method vs standalone
docs.text:
A kernel declared as a method of a @cm.template class is called on the instance (self.mutate(...)), which resolves the model's compile options; a module-level kernel is called directly. Both compile on first use, and both can be inspected:

model = MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True)
print(model.prepare())        # {"mutate": ["none(Array(float64, 2, C), ...)"]}

See Compilation options for what the model contributes and Troubleshooting when a kernel compiles with unexpected options.

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
• First call pays the compile. Warm up with model.prepare() or solve(..., prepare=True) before timing.
  • cache=True (decorator kwarg or model flag) writes Numba's on-disk cache, skipping compilation on the next process.
  • Keep dtypes stable. A float32 argument into a float64 spec upcasts (one copy, one signature); a mix of dtypes compiles several signatures.
  • Avoid Python objects (lists, dicts, strings) inside the body — Numba's nopython mode rejects them.

docs.title: @cm.reduce (guvectorize)
docs.text:
@cm.reduce maps to numba.guvectorize: a generalized ufunc that loops over named core dimensions and writes into an output array Numba allocates for you. It is the tool for row-wise and matrix kernels where the loop over the data is the whole point but the layout is regular.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.reduce
def clip(row: "Array[float, 'n']",
         low: "Scalar[float]",
         up: "Scalar[float]",
         out: "Array[float, 'n']"):
    for i in range(row.shape[0]):
        out[i] = min(max(row[i], low), up)


clip(np.array([[-5.0, 0.5, 5.0], [10.0, -10.0, 1.0]]), -1.0, 1.0)
# -> array([[-1. ,  0.5,  1. ], [ 1. , -1. ,  1. ]])

The last parameter is the output: it is allocated by Numba and never passed in by the caller.

docs.title: Three forms
docs.text: Form When Typed annotations (preferred) layout inferred from dimension labels; last parameter is the output cm.Contract you want explicit control over core types and layout Legacy (signatures, layout) porting existing guvectorize code

docs.title: 1. Annotation-inferred (preferred)
docs.text:
Every parameter must be annotated with a fully typed spec, and the dimension labels define the layout:

@cm.reduce
def matmul(a: "Array[float, 'm,n']",
           b: "Array[float, 'n,k']",
           out: "Array[float, 'm,k']"):
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):
        for j in range(b.shape[1]):
            acc = 0.0
            for k in range(a.shape[1]):
                acc += a[i, k] * b[k, j]
            out[i, j] = acc

Here n is shared between a and b (a core dimension that must match), while m and k are free — Numba loops over them and allocates the result.

You can add an explicit layout= alongside annotations:

@cm.reduce(layout="(n),()->(n)")
def scale(row: "Array[float, 1]", factor: "Scalar[float]",
          out: "Array[float, 1]"):
    ...

docs.title: 2. cm.Contract
docs.text:
Contract[[inputs...], output] encodes the same information without annotations, with shorthands (see specs):

@cm.reduce(cm.Contract[[float, float, ..., ..., ...], float])
def combine(a, b, s1, s2, s3, out):
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):
        out[i] = a[i] + b[i] * (s1 + s2 + s3)
# layout: (n),(n),(),(),()->(n)
  • A plain dtype (float) means Array[dtype, "n"] — a 1-D array.
  • ... means a scalar.
  • Array[dtype] without a rank gets a private dimension (k0, …), shared with nothing.

docs.title: 3. Legacy (signatures, layout)
docs.text:
The classic Numba form, still accepted — and the way to declare multiple signatures:

@cm.reduce(
    [
        [cm.Array[float, 1], cm.Scalar[float], cm.Array[float, 1]],
        [cm.Array[np.float32, 1], cm.Scalar[float], cm.Array[np.float32, 1]],
    ],
    "(n),()->(n)",
)
def scale(row, factor, out):
    for i in range(row.shape[0]):
        out[i] = row[i] * factor

docs.title: Layout rules
docs.text:
• Every parameter is fully typed — a bare cm.Array raises.
  • Dimension labels are matched by name across all arguments, including the output.
  • Every output dimension must appear in some input.
  • The output cannot be a scalar — a gufunc always writes into an array.
  • Scalars are annotated cm.Scalar[dtype] and appear as () in the layout.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Effect fastmath=True Numba fastmath parallel=True target="parallel" — parallel over the free dimensions any other kwarg forwarded verbatim (cache=True, …)

For a model method, the flags can also come from the model (Compilation options).

docs.title: Choosing between reduce, vectorize and precompile
docs.text: You are writing… Use scalar → scalar, broadcast @cm.vectorize a loop over core dimensions with a matching output layout @cm.reduce anything irregular: branches over rows, multiple outputs, early exits @cm.precompile a whole-block objective (pop, ndim) -> (pop,) @cm.precompile + cm.vectorized_target

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
model = MyModel(seed=1)
print(cm.prepare(model))       # {"scale": ["(float64,)->(float64)", ...]}

@cm.reduce kernels compile at decoration time when fully typed, so signature errors surface at import. See Troubleshooting for the common TypeErrors.

docs.title: Typing and cast specs
docs.text: Numba compiles on concrete types, not on Python type hints. The spec markers tell cmenpy two things at once: how to cast each argument before the call (dtype, memory layout) and how to type it inside Numba (dtype, rank). Plain hints (npt.NDArray[np.float64]) are ignored — only markers count.

docs.title: cm.Array — array parameters
docs.text:
cm.Array                      # untyped: np.asarray, any dtype/rank
cm.Array[float]               # float64, rank inferred as 1 by default in Contract
cm.Array[float, 2]            # float64, rank 2 (C-contiguous)
cm.Array[float, "m,n"]        # float64, rank 2, dimensions named
cm.Array[float, 2, "F"]       # float64, rank 2, Fortran-contiguous
Subscript Meaning dtype NumPy dtype the argument is coerced to ndim integer rank or a string of comma-separated dimension labels layout "C" (default), "F" or "A" (any) — the memory layout

docs.title: cm.Scalar — scalar parameters
docs.text:
cm.Scalar            # untyped: coerced with float()
cm.Scalar[float]     # float64 scalar
cm.Scalar[int]       # int64 scalar

docs.title: cm.Contract — full signatures for @cm.reduce
docs.text:
cm.Contract[[float, float, ..., ..., ...], float]     # (n),(n),(),(),()->(n)
cm.Contract[[cm.Array[float, "m,n"], cm.Array[float, "n,k"]],
            cm.Array[float, "m,k"]]                   # (m,n),(n,k)->(m,k)

Contract[[inputs...], output] encodes both the core types and the layout; @cm.reduce reads it directly. See reduce for the shorthand rules.

docs.title: Where specs go
docs.text:
Specs can be passed positionally to the decorator or declared as parameter annotations. All of these are equivalent:

# 1. Positional specs (win over any annotation).
@cm.precompile(cm.Array[float, 2], cm.Scalar[float])
def hunt(X, a): ...

# 2. String annotations.
@cm.precompile
def hunt(X: "Array[float, 2]", a: "Scalar[float]"): ...

# 3. typing.Annotated with a marker (mypy/pyright-clean).
@cm.precompile
def hunt(X: typing.Annotated[npt.NDArray[np.float64], cm.Array[float, 2]],
         a: typing.Annotated[float, cm.Scalar[float]]): ...

# 4. typing.Annotated with a string marker.
@cm.precompile
def hunt(X: typing.Annotated[np.ndarray, "Array[float, 2]"]): ...

Rules:

  • Positional specs win over annotations, and a raw numba signature string (e.g. "float64(float64, float64)") wins over everything.
  • A plain type hint is not a spec — it is ignored, and the kernel stays untyped (lazy).
  • String annotations are resolved in the function's globals plus Array and Scalar, so from __future__ import annotations and stringified hints work.
  • In annotations use the bare names Array/Scalar (they are injected into the namespace); positional specs use cm.Array/cm.Scalar.

docs.title: What casting does
docs.text:
Casting runs before the compiled call, on every argument, following its spec:

Spec Scalar input Array input cm.Array (untyped) np.asarray(value) np.asarray(value) cm.Array[float] np.ascontiguousarray(value, dtype=float64) same cm.Array[float, 2, "F"] np.asfortranarray(value, dtype=float64) same cm.Scalar float(value) float(value) cm.Scalar[float] np.dtype(float64).type(value) np.dtype(float64).type(value)

Consequences worth knowing:

  • A Python list becomes an array (cm.Array kernels accept lists).
  • A float32 array passed to a cm.Array[float, 2] kernel is upcast — the float64 signature is the only one compiled.
  • A Fortran-ordered array passed to a "C" kernel is copied into C order.
  • Casting can allocate; in a hot inner loop pass already-typed arrays and avoid specs that force a copy.

docs.title: Eager vs lazy compilation
docs.text:
A spec is typed when it has both a dtype and a rank:

  • All specs typed → the kernel compiles at decoration time.
  • Any spec untyped (cm.Array, cm.Array[float] without rank) → the kernel stays lazy and compiles on first call, when numba sees the concrete arguments.
@cm.precompile(cm.Array[float, 2])     # compiled at import
def total(A): ...

@cm.precompile(cm.Array)               # lazy: compiles on first call
def total(A): ...

The trade-off: eager kernels surface signature errors immediately and can be inspected with cm.prepare; lazy kernels compile once per concrete argument type they meet.

docs.title: Contract shorthand
docs.text:
Inside cm.Contract:

  • A plain dtype (float, np.float32) means Array[dtype, "n"] — a 1-D array.
  • ... means a default-float scalar.
  • Array[dtype] (no rank) gets a private dimension (k0, k1, …) — a per-argument axis that shares nothing with other arguments.
  • Named dimensions ("m,n") are shared by name across all arguments.
  • Every output dimension must appear in some input, and the output cannot be a scalar.
cm.Contract[[float, cm.Array[float]], float]     # (n),(k0)->(n): private k0
cm.Contract[[float, cm.Array[float, "m"]], cm.Array[float, "n,m"]]   # (n),(m)->(n,m)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom → cause → fix, using the messages the decorators actually raise.

docs.title: Precompiled @cm.vectorize needs a full signature
docs.text:
A @cm.vectorize kernel was given positional specs with a dtype but no full signature (the return type is missing). A ufunc must know its result dtype before it compiles.

@cm.vectorize(cm.Scalar[float])        # TypeError
def bad(r, a): ...

# fix — return dtype first, then the argument list:
@cm.vectorize(cm.Scalar[float, [cm.Scalar[float], cm.Scalar[float]]])
def good(r, a): ...

docs.title: Precompiled @cm.vectorize with annotations needs a typed return
docs.text:
Same cause, annotation form: parameters are typed but the return is not.

@cm.vectorize
def bad(x: "Scalar[float]"): ...       # TypeError

@cm.vectorize
def good(x: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]": ...

Either annotate the return, pass the full positional signature, or drop the annotations and let the kernel stay lazy.

docs.title: cm.reduce needs signatures or fully typed parameter annotations
docs.text:
A @cm.reduce kernel has neither a signature form nor usable annotations. reduce always needs a complete layout — give one of the three forms (described in reduce):

@cm.reduce(layout="(n),()->(n)")            # annotations + layout
@cm.reduce(cm.Contract[[float, float], float])   # Contract
@cm.reduce([cm.Array[float, 1], cm.Scalar[float],
            cm.Array[float, 1]], "(n),()->(n)")   # legacy signatures

docs.title: cm.reduce requires fully typed parameter annotations
docs.text:
Some parameter is untyped or bare (cm.Array with no dtype). Every reduce parameter — including the output — must carry dtype and dims:

@cm.reduce
def bad(row: "Array[float]", out: "Array[float, 'n']"): ...   # TypeError

@cm.reduce
def good(row: "Array[float, 'n']", out: "Array[float, 'n']"): ...

docs.title: cm.reduce requires fully typed specs, e.g. cm.Array[float, 1] or cm.Scalar[float]
docs.text: The legacy form got a bare marker. Add dtypes to every entry of the signature list.

docs.title: Layout '(n),()->(n)' expects 2 inputs, but 3 specs were given
docs.text: The layout string and the signature disagree on arity. Count: (...)->(...) means every atom before -> is an input (including scalars ()), and the atom after it is the output — the output is also one of the specs.

docs.title: Contract errors
docs.text: Message Cause Fix Contract array and scalar specs need a dtype, e.g. Array[float]. bare Array or Scalar inside a Contract Array[float, "n"], Scalar[float] Unsupported Contract spec: <value>. entry that is not a dtype, ..., Array[...] or Scalar[...] use one of the shorthands (specs) cm.Contract does not support a scalar output; use an Array[...]. output is a scalar a gufunc always writes an array — Array[...] output Contract output dimensions ['m'] do not appear in any input. an output dimension label is not in any input output dims must be a subset of input dims; fix the labels The first Contract argument must be a list of specs. Contract[[...], out] written without the inner list keep the [[inputs...], output] shape

docs.title: Numba TypingError: No implementation of function ... found
docs.text:
The compiled body does not match the declared spec. Check in order:

  • actual dtype vs declared (float32 argument into a float64 spec is cast, but a scalar spec applied to an array casts to a scalar — usually not what you meant);
  • rank vs declared (cm.Array[float, 2] on a 1-D array fails inside the body);
  • unsupported constructs in the body (Python objects, dynamic attributes) — Numba's nopython mode rejects them (precompile).

docs.title: Target is not vectorized; wrap it withvectorized_target.
docs.text: Raised by TargetFunction.evaluate_matrix when the objective is not marked vectorized. Wrap it with cm.vectorized_target, or give your callable a vectorized = True attribute. See Vectorized targets.

docs.title: Parallel has no effect
docs.text:
• @cm.precompile: the body must use nb.prange. A plain range loop compiles and runs serially.
  • Model method: for precompile the kernel must also opt in — declaring the method with @cm.precompile and setting only model=parallel=True is not enough (options).
  • ufuncs (vectorize/reduce) do not need prange; they use target="parallel".

docs.title: A kernel compiles with the wrong options
docs.text:
Class-level or standalone access ignores the model's flags:

MyModel.mutate            # decorator options only
model = MyModel(parallel=True)
model.mutate              # sees the model options

Call the kernel on an instance. Confirm with kernel.targetoptions.

docs.title: The first call is slow
docs.text: That is the compilation. Warm up with model.prepare(), cm.prepare(model), or solve(..., prepare=True), and set cache=True (decorator or model flag) to reuse Numba's on-disk cache across processes.

docs.title: Several signatures compile unexpectedly
docs.text: Each distinct resolved option set compiles its own variant, and each distinct concrete argument type compiles its own signature. If you see extra signatures, check for mixed dtypes reaching a cast spec, or a model and a decorator disagreeing on fastmath/cache across calls. Inspect with kernel.signatures().

docs.title: Debugging checklist
docs.text:
model = MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True)

print(model.prepare())          # {name: [signatures]} across the MRO
print(model.compile_options)    # what the model contributes

k = model.mutate                # resolve through the instance
print(k.signatures())           # compiled signatures
print(k.targetoptions)          # merged numba options

For a module-level kernel use cm.kernels(Cls) / kernel.signatures() directly.

docs.title: @cm.vectorize (ufunc)
docs.text:
@cm.vectorize maps to numba.vectorize. It turns a scalar kernel — one value in, one value out — into a NumPy ufunc that broadcasts over arrays.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.vectorize
def double(x: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return 2.0 * x


double(np.array([1.0, 2.0]))        # -> array([2., 4.])

The decorated kernel is a np.ufunc: it broadcasts, accepts scalars, and can be passed anywhere NumPy expects one.

docs.title: Signatures: the full-signature rule
docs.text:
A ufunc must know its return dtype before it is compiled. @cm.vectorize accepts a full eager signature in four ways:

# 1. Positional _Signature — return dtype first, then the argument list.
@cm.vectorize(cm.Scalar[float, [cm.Scalar[float], cm.Scalar[float]]])
def affine(r, a):
    return a * r + 1.0

# 2. Typed return annotation (all params typed too).
@cm.vectorize
def affine(r: "Scalar[float]", a: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return a * r + 1.0

# 3. Raw numba signature string.
@cm.vectorize("float64(float64, float64)")
def add(x, y):
    return x + y

# 4. Bare / partially typed — deferred; numba infers at the first call.
@cm.vectorize
def affine(r: "Array", a: "Scalar"):
    return a * r + 1.0

Partially typed and precompiling raises

A kernel that has some typed specs but no typed return cannot be eagerly compiled:

@cm.vectorize
def bad(x: "Scalar[float]"):     # TypeError: needs a typed return
    return x

Either annotate the return (-> "Scalar[float]"), give the full positional signature, or drop the annotations and let it stay lazy.

A raw numba signature string wins over any annotation.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Effect fastmath=True Numba fastmath parallel=True target="parallel" — NumPy parallel ufunc; no prange needed any other kwarg forwarded verbatim (cache=True, nopython=True, …)

nopython is forced on. For a model method, parallel/fastmath/cache can also come from the model — see Compilation options.

docs.title: Clip to bounds
docs.text:
The canonical use inside an optimizer body — no loops, pure scalar math:

@cm.vectorize
def clip(x: "Scalar[float]", lo: "Scalar[float]", hi: "Scalar[float]") \
        -> "Scalar[float]":
    return min(max(x, lo), hi)


pop.compute << clip(~pop.extract, ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up)

docs.title: Affine scaling
docs.text:
@cm.vectorize
def scale(x: "Scalar[float]", a: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return a * x

docs.title: Gaussian perturbation of one coordinate
docs.text:
@cm.vectorize
def perturb(x: "Scalar[float]", noise: "Scalar[float]",
            s: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return x + s * noise

docs.title: Activation-style helper
docs.text:
@cm.vectorize(fastmath=True)
def sigmoid(x: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))

docs.title: @cm.vectorize vs @cm.precompile for objectives
docs.text: Do not use @cm.vectorize for a whole-block objective. A ufunc maps one scalar to one scalar — it cannot turn (pop, ndim) into (pop,). For an objective that scores a block, use @cm.precompile plus cm.vectorized_target.

docs.title: Method vs standalone
docs.text:
Identical to precompile: a @cm.template method receives the model's compile options at instantiation, a module-level kernel uses the decorator's. Introspection is the same — model.prepare(), cm.kernels, .signatures().

model = MyModel(seed=1, parallel=True)
print(model.prepare())        # {"clip": ["float64(float64, float64, float64)"]}

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
A model is an optimizer you describe once and then run against any objective. cmenpy offers two declaration styles that produce the same contract — a callable exposing:

(best_fitness, best_x) = model.solve(
    f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min"
)
  • @cm.declare wraps a function: one body drives the whole run, and parameters are bound by keyword.
  • @cm.template wraps a class: per-instance state, an explicit initialize/evolve split, fields, and numba kernels that inherit compile options.

Both produce a BaseOptimizer with .solve(...), .alias and .tracker.

docs.title: Where and when to use which
docs.text:
@cm.declare (function) @cm.template (class) Run structure one function body; you iterate the epochs yourself initialize once, then evolve per epoch Parameters cm.Argument only, keyword-bound at call time cm.Argument, cm.Variable, cm.Constant Per-instance state closure/local variables only instance attributes (self.w) Numba kernels module-level (decorator options only) methods that receive the model's compile options Compile options none parallel / fastmath / cache at instantiation Reuse/composition copy/paste or plain functions inheritance and @cm.module Operator Modules Introspection alias, tracker plus model_class, compile_options, prepare() Best for scripts, quick experiments, one-off algorithms reusable optimizers, anything with state or kernels

Choose @cm.declare when the algorithm is a single function, you want parameters bound by keyword, and you have no per-instance state or compiled kernels needing model options. It is the shortest path from idea to run.

Choose @cm.template when you want the initialize/evolve split, keep state across epochs on self, declare constants, compile numba kernels that should honor parallel/fastmath/cache, share operators through @cm.module, or introspect/prepare the model.

The same algorithm in both styles:

@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def random_search(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                   (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))
    for _ in epoch:
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                       (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))


@cm.template
class RandomSearch:
    x: cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2]

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                       (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                       (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Function style — one pass:

@cm.declare → FunctionOptimizerModel
model = algo(x=1)                       # bind fields (+ optional seed)
solve(...)  → build context
            → func(args=args, epoch=epoch_it, ctx=Context(...))   # once
            → you iterate `epoch`; ctx.epoch stays 0
            → return (best_fitness, best_x)

Class style — per-epoch hooks:

@cm.template → TemplateOptimizerModel (class wrapped, not yet instantiated)
model = MyAlgorithm(x=1, seed=1)        # instantiate: bind fields + options
solve(..., prepare=False) → [prepare(): compile kernels]
                          → initialize(ctx)                # once
                          → for e in epoch_it: evolve(e, ctx=Context(...))
                          → return (best_fitness, best_x)

A fresh Context is built for every hook call in the class style, so ctx.epoch tracks the current epoch. In the function style the single Context is built before your function runs — use the epoch iterator's counter, not ctx.epoch, inside @cm.declare.

docs.title: solve parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Meaning f the objective; any callable, optionally wrapped with cm.vectorized_target bounds a Bounds or a bounds sequence; defines ndim epochs total epochs (iterated as 0 .. epochs-1) pop_size initial population size pop_range (min, max) allowed sizes for dynamic populations debug record per-epoch history in model.tracker sense "min" (default) or "max" prepare (template only) compile the class's kernels before running

Returns (best_fitness, best_x) — the best row of the buffer, respecting sense.

Planned for 2026b2

solve will accept two opt-in run-control arguments alongside these: terminator= for composable stopping criteria (#33) and history= for in-memory / on-disk run records (#35). Today the equivalents are the fixed epochs cap and debug=True with model.tracker.

docs.title: The ctx object
docs.text:
Every hook receives a read-only Context:

Attribute Meaning ctx.bounds the search space (low, up, ndim) ctx.buff the KernelBuffer backing the population ctx.rng seeded random generator ctx.sense "min" or "max" ctx.epoch / ctx.epochs current epoch / total (template style) ctx.target the wrapped objective (budget accounting lives on the run's own wrapper)

Per-dimension bounds

bounds.low / bounds.up are the first dimension's scalars. For unequal per-dimension intervals pass the arrays straight to the sampler (e.g. an opfunu objective's f.lb / f.ub — see Test functions). Bounds.lows, ups, sample() and clip() helpers land in 2026b2 (#37).
