docs.title: Function style (@cm.declare)
docs.text:
@cm.declare turns a function into a model. The function receives (args, epoch, ctx) and drives the whole run inside its body — you iterate the epochs yourself.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def my_algorithm(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                   (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

    for _ in epoch:                       # one epoch per iteration
        pop.compute << np.clip(
            ~pop.extract
            + ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)) * args.x,
            ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
        )

The decorated name is the model (FunctionOptimizerModel).

docs.title: The function contract
docs.text:
The function is called by keyword with exactly three parameters:

Parameter What it is args the bound field values (args.x, args.lr, …) epoch an EpochIteration — iterate it to run epochs ctx the per-run Context

Name the parameters exactly args, epoch, ctx — the runner passes them by keyword.

docs.title: epoch
docs.text:
for _ in epoch:            # yields 0, 1, ..., epochs-1
    ...

epoch.max                  # total epochs
epoch.current              # index of the epoch most recently yielded
epoch.cpu_time             # wall CPU time spent so far

The iterator tracks per-epoch CPU time, and with debug=True also records a history snapshot per epoch.

docs.title: ctx
docs.text: One Context is built before your function runs and lives for the whole run. ctx.epoch is therefore fixed at 0 in this style — read progress from the epoch iterator instead.

docs.title: Declaring and binding parameters
docs.text:
@cm.declare(
    x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2],        # range-checked with a default
    lr=cm.Argument[float, (0.0, 1.0)],    # required at binding time
)
def my_algorithm(args, epoch, ctx): ...

Declare fields by keyword — positional declarations passed to the decorator (or values passed positionally at binding) are ignored by the current implementation.

model = my_algorithm(seed=7, x=1, lr=0.1)   # seed first, then fields
model.solve(f, bounds, epochs=100, pop_size=20)
  • seed is the first parameter of the binding call; it seeds the run's ctx.rng.
  • Every field with a range and no default must be bound; a field that was declared but never bound raises AttributeError when read through args.
  • Only cm.Argument is supported — see Fields. cm.Constant raises at declaration time (it is a class-style feature).

docs.title: Errors at binding
docs.text:
Error When AttributeError: Cannot initialize 'y': It was not declared in MyArguments. binding an undeclared name TypeError: Invalid type in arguments: Invalid type for 'x'. Expected int, got str type mismatch ValueError: Invalid value in arguments: Value 5 for 'x' out of range [0, 3]. outside the range AttributeError: Attribute 'lr' has been declared but not initialized yet. reading an unbound field through args

Range checks also cover arrays and collections (every element must be in range).

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
    f, bounds, epochs=100, pop_size=20,
    pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min",
)

model.alias                     # the function's __name__
model.tracker                   # [] unless solve(debug=True)

Each solve builds a fresh run (new buffer, new RNG, new tracker). Calling solve again on the same model rebinds the seed/fields only if you call the model again; the field values persist.

model = my_algorithm(x=1)                 # one configuration...
a = model.solve(f, bounds, 100, 20)       # ...run against many objectives
b = model.solve(g, bounds, 200, 40)

docs.title: Kernels and the function style
docs.text: The function style has no compile-option channel: there is no parallel/fastmath/cache to pass at binding time. Numba kernels used by a @cm.declare model are declared at module level and compile with their decorator's own options — see Numba kernels and Compilation options.

docs.title: Limitations at a glance
docs.text:
• fields: cm.Argument only (no Constant, no Variable);
  • state: locals/closures, no per-instance attributes;
  • no prepare() / compile options;
  • ctx.epoch is fixed at 0.

If you need any of these, use the class style.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: example/hello_world_v1.py is the complete, runnable version of the algorithm above.

docs.title: Fields and markers
docs.text:
Model fields are declared as class annotations (or @cm.declare keyword declarations) using three subscript-only markers. Each marker builds a typing.Annotated type whose metadata carries the field's rules — that is why fields are validated at declaration/binding time and read like plain attributes afterwards.

class MyAlgorithm:
    w: cm.Argument[float, (0.1, 1.0), 0.5]   # tunable
    pbest: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]           # internal state
    P: cm.Constant[int, 100]                 # fixed

docs.title: cm.Argument — tunable parameters
docs.text:
Form Meaning cm.Argument[type] required at binding; no range cm.Argument[type, default] default value when not bound cm.Argument[type, (min, max)] range-checked, required cm.Argument[type, (min, max), default] range-checked with a default 
@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    a: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100)]            # must be bound
    b: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100), 5]         # defaults to 5


MyAlgorithm(a=3)             # ok
MyAlgorithm()                # TypeError: Missing required argument: 'a'
MyAlgorithm(a=0)             # ValueError: Value 0 out of range for 'a'
MyAlgorithm(a="x")           # TypeError: Field 'a' must be of type int

An unsupported subscript raises TypeError listing the four valid forms.

Validation is stricter for range-declared fields: those get the type check, the range check and the default fallback. A field declared as cm.Argument[type] (or cm.Variable[type]) is stored as given — its annotation documents intent but is not enforced at construction.

In the function style, binding validates every declared field's type, and its range when one is declared; errors surface as TypeError / ValueError (see declare).

docs.title: cm.Variable — internal state
docs.text:
w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

Variable marks state that is not a tunable parameter: no range, no default, nothing required. It is stored as None until you assign it (in initialize or evolve). Use it for personal-best arrays, weights, caches — anything the algorithm maintains rather than the user configures.

docs.title: cm.Constant — fixed values
docs.text:
P: cm.Constant[int, 100]
  • The value is type-checked once at declaration: a mismatch raises TypeError (with numeric widening — an int value satisfies a float constant, mirroring the field casters).
  • It is installed as a read-only class descriptor: readable as self.P and MyAlgorithm.P, but reassignment or deletion raises AttributeError.
  • It is never a constructor parameter — passing it to the constructor raises TypeError.
  • Inherited through the MRO (an Operator Module's constants reach every model that mixes it in), and a subclass may redeclare the name to override the value.

Constants are a class-style feature: @cm.declare rejects them at declaration with TypeError: Constant field 'P' is not supported by cm.declare; ....

docs.title: Choosing a marker
docs.text: You want… Use a knob the user sets (lr, pop factor) cm.Argument a knob with a sensible default cm.Argument[type, default] or the range+default form algorithm state the run maintains cm.Variable a fixed hyperparameter shared by every run/model cm.Constant

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Annotations are resolved at declaration (typing.get_type_hints with include_extras=True), so stringified annotations and from __future__ import annotations work — the marker objects must be importable in the class's module namespace.
  • initialize and evolve are excluded from field processing; a field named like them is not bound.
  • Positional binding follows declaration order (constants skipped) — prefer keywords (template).
  • Numeric widening applies to constants (int → float); the range-declared field checks use strict isinstance.

docs.title: Operator modules
docs.text:
An Operator Module is a Ruby-style mixin: a bundle of kernels, helper methods and fields that any number of @cm.template models can share by inheriting from it.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.module
class MutationOps:
    """A reusable Gaussian-mutation operator module."""

    scale: cm.Constant[float, 0.3]              # shared, read-only

    @cm.vectorize
    def clip(x: cm.Array, lo: cm.Scalar, hi: cm.Scalar):
        return min(max(x, lo), hi)

    def mutate(self, parents, rng):
        noise = rng.standard_normal(parents.shape)
        return self.clip(parents + self.scale * noise, -1.0, 1.0)

@cm.template
class HillClimber(MutationOps):
    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        trial = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff.snapshot)
        trial.compute << self.mutate(~pop.extract, ctx.rng)

        mask = cm.is_best((trial.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
        pop.assign[mask] << trial.access[mask]

HillClimber now has self.scale, self.clip and self.mutate without duplicating a line.

docs.title: What @cm.module does
docs.text:
• keeps the class identity — it returns the same class;
  • materializes cm.Constant annotations as read-only descriptors immediately, so MutationOps.scale works even before any model includes the mixin;
  • rejects non-classes with TypeError (a @cm.template model instance is not reusable as a mixin).

Mixin application is ordinary inheritance: a module can hold anything a base class can — cm.Argument / cm.Variable / cm.Constant fields, all three kernel decorators, plain helper methods.

docs.title: MRO rules
docs.text:
Collisions resolve through the normal MRO, leftmost base wins:

@cm.template
class Hybrid(FastMutation, SlowMutation):   # FastMutation's operators win
    ...

A subclass redefinition always wins over any base, module or not. Constants follow the same rule, and redeclaring the name in a subclass overrides the inherited value.

docs.title: Kernels and compile options
docs.text:
Kernels declared in a module are inherited exactly like methods: called through the model instance (self.clip(...)), they compile with the model's compile options; accessed on the module class they use the decorator's. model.prepare() / cm.prepare walk the MRO, so inherited kernels are reported and warmed up with the model's options too.

model = HillClimber(seed=1, fastmath=True)
model.prepare()          # {"clip": [...], ...} — includes the module's clip

See Compilation options.

docs.title: Composition patterns
docs.text:
• Keep modules stateless. Let the model own the state (cm.Variable) and the module own behavior plus cm.Constant hyperparameters.
  • One concern per module — MutationOps, SelectionOps, CrossoverOps — composed by listing bases: class GA(SelectionOps, CrossoverOps):.
  • Temper constants in the model when the fixed value is only a baseline:
step = self.scale * (1.0 - e / ctx.epochs)     # Annealer in the example

docs.title: When to use a module vs a plain base class
docs.text: @cm.module is not required for inheritance — a plain base class works almost the same. Use it when you want constants installed (and validated) at decoration time, so MutationOps.scale is reachable on the mixin itself before any model includes it. Use a plain base class when the "mixin" is really a template itself.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text: example/operator_module.py defines MutationOps once and builds two models (HillClimber, Annealer) on top of it, runnable side by side.

docs.title: Class style (@cm.template)
docs.text:
@cm.template turns a class into a model. The class supplies initialize(self, ctx) and evolve(self, e, ctx); the model handles validation, the epoch loop, tracking and kernel compilation.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    a: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100)]                 # tunable, range-checked

    w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]                    # internal state (starts None)

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                       (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))
        self.w = np.zeros(ctx.bounds.ndim)

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << np.clip(
            ~pop.extract + ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)),
            ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
        )


model = MyAlgorithm(a=3, seed=1)                  # instantiate, then:
best = model.solve(f, bounds, epochs=100, pop_size=20)

@cm.template returns a TemplateOptimizerModel wrapping the class. The model is not instantiated until you call it.

docs.title: Class shape
docs.text: Member Required Role initialize(self, ctx) no (checked with hasattr) one-off setup, runs once per solve evolve(self, e, ctx) yes one epoch of the algorithm fields — cm.Argument / cm.Variable / cm.Constant (fields) kernels — @cm.precompile / @cm.vectorize / @cm.reduce methods helpers — plain methods and Operator modules

docs.title: Instantiation
docs.text:
model = MyAlgorithm(seed=1, a=3, parallel=True, cache=True)

The binding call is model(seed=None, *args, **kwargs):

  • seed is the first positional; keyword use is recommended.
  • Remaining keywords are field values (plus compile options).
  • Positional values after the seed bind to fields in declaration order (MyAlgorithm(1, 4) → seed=1, first field =4); constants are skipped, which makes positional binding fragile — prefer keywords.

The generated __init__ then:

  1. pops the compile options (parallel/fastmath/cache) — see Compilation options;
  2. reads the class's Annotated type hints and validates each field (type, range, required-vs-default);
  3. sets the fields as instance attributes;
  4. delegates to the class's own __init__, if it has one (compile options are not forwarded to it).

docs.title: Errors at instantiation
docs.text: Error When TypeError: Missing required argument: 'x' a range-declared field with no default and no value TypeError: Field 'x' must be of type int type mismatch ValueError: Value 5 out of range for 'x' outside (min, max) TypeError: Constant field 'P' cannot be passed to the constructor; it is fixed at declaration. passing a Constant

docs.title: Lifecycle of a run
docs.text:
model.solve(f, bounds, epochs, pop_size,
            pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min", prepare=False)
  1. prepare=True → all kernels of the class compile up front with the model's options.
  2. A context is built: buffer, bounds, seeded RNG, tracker.
  3. initialize(ctx) runs once — seed the population here.
  4. evolve(e, ctx) runs for e in 0 .. epochs-1. A fresh Context is built for every epoch, so ctx.epoch tracks the current epoch.
  5. The best row of the buffer is returned as (best_fitness, best_x).

Because state lives on self, a second solve on the same model reuses the instance: initialize runs again, but stale self attributes persist unless you reset them there.

docs.title: Kernels as methods
docs.text:
@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    @cm.precompile(parallel=True)
    def mutate(self, K: "Array[float, 2]", s: "Scalar[float]"):
        out = np.empty_like(K)
        for i in range(K.shape[0]):
            for j in range(K.shape[1]):
                out[i, j] = K[i, j] + s * (2.0 * (i % 3) - 1.0)
        return out

Called through the instance (self.mutate(...), model.mutate(...)), the kernel inherits the model's compile options; accessed on the class (MyAlgorithm.mutate) it uses the decorator's. Operator-module kernels mixed into the class behave identically.

docs.title: Introspection and warm-up
docs.text:
model.alias                     # "MyAlgorithm"
model.model_class               # the wrapped class
model.compile_options           # {"parallel": True, "fastmath": False, ...}
model.prepare()                 # force compilation, {kernel: [signatures]}
model.tracker                   # [] unless solve(debug=True)

solve(..., prepare=True) compiles inside the run — the right default before benchmarking or production runs.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text: Plain base classes work as usual (fields, methods and kernels are inherited). For cross-cutting operators shared by several models, prefer @cm.module Operator Modules.

docs.text: example/hello_world_v2.py is a runnable model in this style; the Build a custom model tutorial implements a complete (μ + λ) Evolution Strategy step by step.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
cm.PopulationSwarm(buffer) is the handle you write algorithm bodies with. Underneath it is a KernelBuffer: one flat (pop_size, ndim + 1) array where column 0 is the fitness and columns 1: are the solution vector — one row per individual, laid out the way Numba kernels want it.

pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)   # pop.X = solutions, pop.F = fitness

docs.title: What the swarm composes
docs.text:
PopulationSwarm is four mixins over the same buffer:

Mixin Provides StreamOperations the DSL verbs: compute, assign, access, extract BufferMatrixOperations the views X, F, idx, size BaseIterator for i in pop, best, worst, sort DynamicBase roster: insert, remove, free_space

docs.title: The buffer model
docs.text:
• The buffer is allocated to the maximum population size (pop_range); pop.size is the number of active rows.
  • A row is active while it holds a live individual; pop.remove(i) deactivates it and fills it with NaN, and pop.insert(x) reuses the first free row.
  • Fitness lives in column 0, so every row is a self-contained (fitness, solution) record — that is what makes whole-row copies and block scoring cheap.

docs.title: 60-second tour
docs.text:
pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)

# Initialize: write a whole (pop_size, ndim) block and score it.
pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                               (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

best = pop.F[pop.best]                       # fitness of the best individual

for i in pop:                                # every row index
    ...

for _ in epoch:
    # Score offspring: ~pop.X / ~extract are the active solution rows.
    pop.compute << np.clip(~pop.X + ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1,
                                                    (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)),
                           ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up)

    if pop.F[pop.best] < best:               # sense-aware comparison
        pop.remove(pop.worst)                # shrink the roster
    elif pop.free_space:
        pop.insert(ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                   ctx.bounds.ndim))   # grow it

docs.title: I want to…
docs.text: Task Use write solutions and score them pop.compute << values write rows without scoring (raw) pop.assign << values read the solution block pop.X, ~pop.X, pop.extract read whole rows (fitness + solution) pop.access[i], ~pop.access read the fitness column pop.F, ~pop.F find best / worst / rank best, worst, sort iterate individuals for i in pop / for i in ~pop grow or shrink the roster insert / remove / free_space score candidates in isolation ctx.buff.snapshot + assign

  • Stream operators — the << / [] / ~ DSL and recipes.

Full class reference: API Reference → Classes; buffer types under Buffer, comparators under Comparators, Bounds under Search space.

docs.title: Stream operators
docs.text:
The swarm's verbs are four stream operators. Each is a fresh object bound to the buffer, and each is used with << (write), [] (row select), ~ (active rows) and, for readers, >> (pass-through).

Operator Direction Scores? pop.compute write yes — solutions are evaluated against the objective pop.assign write no — raw row write, fitness included pop.access read — whole rows: fitness + solution pop.extract read — solution columns only

docs.title: pop.compute — write and score
docs.text:
pop.compute << values            # score a whole (k, ndim) block, active rows
pop.compute[i] << row            # score one row into row i
pop.compute[mask] << rows        # score the rows a mask or index array selects
pop.compute[~pop] << rows        # score the rows that hold a fitness

compute delegates to KernelBuffer.apply, which writes the solutions and fills column 0 with their fitness:

  • no index → the block is written into the active rows (mask.founds), so inactive (removed) rows are untouched;
  • one row (pop.compute[3], pop.compute[pop.best]) → a single row is written and scored with one objective call; pop.best, pop.worst and pop.sort hand out np.intp indices, which count as one row too;
  • block + vectorized target → one evaluate_matrix call scores the whole block (vectorized targets);
  • block + plain target → row-by-row fallback via apply_along_axis;
  • an empty selection (a mask with nothing set) → nothing is evaluated.

Either way the NFE counter is charged one evaluation per row scored — the same selection costs the same with a plain and with a vectorized objective.

The block you write must broadcast into the selected rows' (k, ndim) shape.

# Initialize / perturb the whole active population.
pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                               (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

# Per-row: re-score row i after an in-place tweak.
pop.compute[pop.best] << new_solution

# Only the improved rows: pay for what you actually re-score.
improved = cm.is_best((offspring.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
pop.compute[improved] << offspring.X[improved]

docs.title: pop.assign — raw write, no scoring
docs.text:
pop.assign << rows      # overwrite the whole buffer (exact shape required)
pop.assign[i] << row    # write one raw row: fitness + solution

assign writes straight into the buffer without touching the objective:

  • the whole-block form raises IndexError unless the value's shape is exactly the buffer shape (max, ndim + 1) — it is meant for restoring captured raw rows, not for solutions;
  • the per-row form writes a full row (fitness + solution). That is the tool for merging already-scored candidates (elitist selection) without paying for a re-evaluation.

Stale fitness

assign never validates the fitness against the solution. If you write solutions through assign, column 0 no longer describes them — use compute unless you are copying rows that were already scored.

docs.title: pop.access — whole-row reader
docs.text:
pop.access[i]           # row i: [fitness, x0, x1, ...]
pop.access[i:j]         # rows i..j-1
~pop.access             # whole rows of the active individuals
other >> pop.access     # pass `other` through (identity)

Use access when a consumer wants the self-contained (fitness, solution) record — for example archiving a row or copying rows between buffers.

docs.title: pop.extract — solution reader
docs.text:
pop.extract[i]          # solution vector of row i (columns 1:)
pop.extract[i:j]        # solution rows i..j-1
~pop.extract            # solutions of the active individuals
other >> pop.extract    # pass-through

~pop.extract is the everyday idiom for "the current solutions" — the input to a mutation step.

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text: pop.compute[i] and pop.assign[i] return pipeline objects rather than the operator itself: they are single-use write targets bound to one row, so the same operator can target any row without re-indexing. A reader's >> is the identity, which lets kernels and helpers be composed in either direction.

docs.title: Score candidates in isolation (snapshot)
docs.text:
Evaluate offspring in a fresh buffer that shares the configuration, then merge only the winners — no re-scoring:

n_pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(buff.snapshot)     # snapshot is a property

n_pop.compute << offspring                     # score in isolation

mask = cm.is_best((n_pop.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask]         # copy winning rows, fitness included

docs.title: Copy selected rows between buffers
docs.text: buff.raw[idx] = pop.access[j]             # whole row, fitness included

docs.title: Grow the roster
docs.text:
if pop.free_space:
    pop.insert(candidate)                # scored and inserted; returns the row

docs.title: Shrink the roster
docs.text:
pop.remove(pop.worst)                     # deactivate + NaN; row reusable

insert/remove and the pop_range sizing that enables them are covered in Iteration and ranking.

docs.title: Iteration and ranking
docs.text: All ordering in the population is sense-aware: with ctx.sense = "min" (smallest fitness first, the default) the lowest fitness is best; with "max" the highest is. Take the sense from ctx.sense and let the ranking API apply it — never hardcode a direction.

docs.title: Iterating
docs.text:
for i in pop:            # every row index of the buffer, 0 .. max-1
    ...

for i in ~pop:           # only rows with a scored (non-NaN) fitness
    ...

~pop yields the indices of rows whose fitness is not NaN — that is, rows that have been scored. A freshly created buffer scores its active rows during initialization, so in practice ~pop and the active roster coincide; the difference appears after remove, where the row becomes NaN and inactive.

To iterate the data instead of the indices, use the views:

for x in ~pop.extract:       # one solution vector at a time (copies)
    ...

pop.access[pop.best]         # the best row: [fitness, x0, x1, ...]

docs.title: best, worst, sort
docs.text:
pop.best          # row index of the best individual
pop.worst         # row index of the worst individual
pop.sort          # row indices ordered best-first

pop.F[pop.best]   # the best fitness value
pop.X[pop.sort[:k]]   # the k best solution vectors

These delegate to the buffer's BufferIndex, which ranks over the fitness column only. Notes:

  • Ties keep the earlier (lower) row first — the ordering is stable.
  • NaN rows sort last in sort and are never best/worst while any scored row exists; on an all-NaN buffer the ranking is meaningless, so initialize before reading it.

pop.idx exposes the same lookups (pop.idx.sort, pop.idx.best, pop.idx.worst, ~pop.idx) plus iteration over the sorted order.

docs.title: Comparators
docs.text:
For element-wise comparisons between two fitness arrays — offspring vs parents, candidates vs personal bests — use the comparators instead of rolling your own:

improved = cm.is_best((new_F, old_F), ctx.sense)     # indices where new wins
worse    = cm.is_worst((new_F, old_F), ctx.sense)    # indices where new loses

best_i   = cm.best_index(F, ctx.sense)   # index of the best entry of F
worst_i  = cm.worst_index(F, ctx.sense)  # index of the worst entry of F
  • is_best/is_worst take a (new, old) pair — a tuple of scalars or arrays — and return the integer indices where the comparison holds. NaN entries never compare, so masked/inactive rows are skipped naturally.
  • is_best(a, sense) == ~is_worst(a, sense) for scored data.
  • best_index/worst_index operate on a single fitness array.

Full reference: API Reference → Comparators.

docs.title: Dynamic sizing
docs.text:
A run can grow and shrink its roster within the bounds given to solve:

model.solve(f, bounds, epochs, pop_size=20, pop_range=(5, 50))

pop_size is the initial size; pop_range sets the minimum and maximum the roster may move between. Within those limits:

pop.size                 # current active individuals
pop.free_space           # True while insert() would succeed

pop.remove(pop.worst)    # deactivate a row: mask off + NaN
idx = pop.insert(x)      # score x into the first free row; returns the row

insert raises ValueError("Max agents in memory.") when no row is free, so guard growth with pop.free_space. The buffer never reallocates: capacity is ctx.buff.size.max.

The classic pattern — remove the worst when a new solution beats it, insert a replacement otherwise — is example/hello_world_v1.py; example/optimizers/de/lshade_algorithm.py shows success-history adaptation over a shrinking roster.

docs.title: Matrix views
docs.text:
The swarm exposes the buffer through four views. They are views: reads and writes go straight to the backing array and take effect immediately.

View Type Contents pop.X read/write the solution block, shape (max, ndim) (buffer columns 1:) pop.F read-only the fitness column, shape (max,) (buffer column 0) pop.idx lookups best/worst/sort over the fitness column pop.size int number of active individuals

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
pop.X[i]          # solution vector of row i
pop.X[i:j]        # solution rows i..j-1
pop.F[i]          # fitness of row i
np.asarray(pop.X) # the whole (max, ndim) block, as an ndarray
np.asarray(pop.F) # the whole fitness column

~ restricts a view to the active rows:

~pop.X            # (active, ndim) solutions of live individuals
~pop.F            # fitness of live individuals

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
pop.X is writable through the scoring operator:

pop.X << values       # score `values` and insert it — same as pop.compute << values

pop.X and pop.F are live views. Read the whole block with pop.X.to_numpy() (or cm.cast(pop.X)) — implicit np.asarray(pop.X) casting is deprecated. They can also be passed directly to cm.precompile/cm.vectorize/cm.reduce kernels (cmenpy unwraps them internally).

pop.F has no write path: fitness is produced by scoring (compute), never assigned directly. To write a raw row (fitness and solution) without scoring, use pop.assign.

np.asarray does not copy

np.asarray(pop.X) and np.asarray(pop.F) return the backing arrays themselves. Mutating the result mutates the population — including its fitness column, which then no longer matches the solutions. Take a copy (.copy()) when you need an isolated array.

docs.title: Live views vs snapshots
docs.text:
pop.X[i]                  # live: reflects every write made since
snap = ctx.buff.snapshot  # a fresh, empty buffer with the same configuration

snapshot is a property returning a new empty KernelBuffer, useful for scoring candidate offspring in isolation before merging them (see operators → recipes).

docs.title: pop.idx — ranked lookups
docs.text:
pop.idx.sort      # row indices ordered best-first (respects ctx.sense)
pop.idx.best      # row index of the best individual
pop.idx.worst     # row index of the worst individual
~pop.idx          # row indices whose fitness is scored (not NaN)
pop.idx[i]        # i-th best row index (iteration is over sort)

All ranking is sense-aware: with sense="min" the lowest fitness is "best"; with sense="max" the highest is. Take the sense from ctx.sense — never hardcode a direction. See Iteration and ranking.

docs.title: pop.size vs capacity
docs.text:
pop.size              # active individuals (int)
ctx.buff.size.max     # capacity: rows the buffer was allocated for
ctx.buff.size.min     # lower bound configured via pop_range
pop.free_space        # True while insert() would succeed

pop.size changes as rows are removed and inserted; the buffer itself never resizes — dynamic populations use pop_range at solve time and remove/insert to move within it. See Iteration and ranking → dynamic sizing.

docs.title: Target functions
docs.text:
A target is the objective you are optimizing. cmenpy accepts any callable that maps one solution vector to one fitness value — a Python function, a compiled kernel, or a whole-block evaluator — and wraps it in a TargetFunction that counts function evaluations (NFE) and enforces an optional budget.

You normally never build the wrapper yourself: solve wraps whatever you pass as the first argument.

model.solve(lambda x: float(np.sum(x**2)), bounds, epochs=100, pop_size=20)

docs.title: The scoring pipeline
docs.text:
Every solution enters the population through the buffer, and the buffer owns the scoring:

new solutions  →  KernelBuffer.apply  →  write column 1:  →  score  →  column 0
                                                  │
                    ┌─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
                    │                             │                          │
            single row (idx int)           vectorized block            plain callable
            one target( ) call             evaluate( ) once            apply_along_axis
            nfe += 1                       nfe += len(block)           nfe += 1 per row

The three paths are what Scoring modes covers; the middle one is the single biggest performance lever in the library.

docs.title: TargetFunction surface
docs.text:
Member Meaning tf(x) / tf.evaluate(x) score row-by-row, spending the budget tf.evaluate_matrix(x) score a whole (pop, ndim) block (vectorized only) tf.nfe evaluations spent so far tf.max the budget (inf when unlimited) tf.bounds the search space tf.vectorized whether the target scores whole blocks

The Target protocol itself is structural: anything callable with x -> float qualifies.

docs.title: Choosing an evaluation mode
docs.text: You have… Mode Page a quick prototype, a cheap objective plain callable, row-by-row Scoring modes a NumPy-level (pop, ndim) -> (pop,) objective vectorized Vectorized targets a Numba-compiled block kernel vectorized + @cm.precompile Vectorized targets several objectives at once multiobjective planned for 2026b2 (#36) a hard cap on evaluations budget NFE budget

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Scoring modes — row-by-row vs whole-block dispatch.
  • Vectorized targets — the contract, examples, pitfalls.
  • NFE budget — max_nfe, MaxNumberOfCalls, accounting.

Full reference: API Reference → Classes and runnable targets in Examples.

docs.title: NFE budget
docs.text: Every scoring call spends from an evaluation counter — the number of function evaluations (NFE) — and a TargetFunction can be given a hard cap (max_nfe) after which it refuses to evaluate anything more.

docs.title: Counter semantics
docs.text:
• Check first, spend after: __spend raises MaxNumberOfCalls when nfe + calls > max, so the counter never exceeds the budget.
  • One individual (tf(x), tf.evaluate(x)) spends 1. A vectorized target gets that solution as a (1, ndim) block and the single score is unwrapped again, so one row never costs ndim.
  • A block (tf.evaluate_matrix(x)) spends len(x) — one per row scored.
  • Row-wise fallback spends 1 per row through the same evaluator.
  • A selection that scores nothing (an empty mask, every row removed) spends 0: the rows are written, the objective is not called.
  • The counter lives on the wrapper, not on your callable, and starts at 0 for every wrapper — a fresh solve gets a fresh counter.

Spelling the same selection with pop.compute costs the same in either scoring mode — the active rows for pop.compute << block, the rows a mask or index array selects, one row for pop.compute[i] (a Python int or the np.intp that pop.best, pop.worst and pop.sort hand out).

docs.title: Setting a budget
docs.text:
from cmenpy.target import TargetFunction

budgeted = TargetFunction(sphere, bounds, max_nfe=10_000)

budgeted.max          # 10000 (np.inf when max_nfe is None)
budgeted.nfe          # evaluations spent so far
budgeted.f            # bound evaluator (same as evaluate)
budgeted.bounds       # the search space

solve builds its own internal wrapper without a budget, so to cap a run pass a pre-wrapped target as the objective — the run's scoring routes through it:

try:
    model.solve(budgeted, bounds, epochs, pop_size)
except MaxNumberOfCalls:
    ...   # budget exhausted mid-run

Planned for 2026b2

Composable terminators — issue #33 — will add a first-class solve(..., terminator=cm.MaxEvaluation(nfe=...)) alongside time-, patience- and target-based criteria. The pre-wrapped TargetFunction stays the low-level equivalent.

docs.title: When the exception fires
docs.text:
MaxNumberOfCalls is raised inside scoring — during an epoch's compute/apply — and propagates out of solve. At that point:

  • the buffer still holds the last completed state (the failing write did not finish);
  • with debug=True, model.tracker.history contains every epoch recorded up to the failure, and each EpochHistory carries its nfe;
  • the exception itself is a plain Exception with the message Max number of function calls exceeded.
from cmenpy.target import MaxNumberOfCalls

try:
    best = model.solve(budgeted, bounds, epochs, pop_size, debug=True)
except MaxNumberOfCalls as e:
    history = model.tracker.history
    print(f"spent {history[-1].nfe} evaluations over {len(history)} epochs")
    raise

docs.title: Reading the NFE of a run
docs.text:
• EpochHistory.nfe (debug=True) — the authoritative cumulative count at the end of each epoch.
  • ctx.target.nfe — not the run's counter. ctx.target is a separate re-wrap created for the context, so its counter only moves if you call through it. Read the run's progress from the tracker instead.

docs.title: Sizing a budget
docs.text: A run scores roughly pop_size solutions per epoch (plus whatever your operators score per epoch), so a first estimate is epochs × pop_size evaluations. Dynamic populations (pop_range, insert/remove) and multi-evaluation operators add to it — measure once with debug=True, then set the cap with headroom.

docs.title: Scoring modes
docs.text:
There are two ways a target is scored, and the difference is the single most important performance lever in cmenpy:

Mode How it scores NFE spent When Row-by-row (default) np.apply_along_axis — one Python call per individual 1 per individual a plain callable Vectorized (fast) one call over the whole (pop, ndim) block len(block) wrapped with cm.vectorized_target

docs.title: Row-by-row
docs.text:
A plain Python callable works as-is:

def sphere(x):                      # x: one solution vector -> one float
    return float(np.sum(x**2))

model.solve(sphere, bounds, epochs, pop_size)     # scored row-by-row

Each epoch, KernelBuffer.apply feeds the active rows through np.apply_along_axis(self.__target, 1, ...): one Python-level call per individual, one NFE each. This is fine for prototypes and cheap objectives; for anything expensive it dominates the runtime.

docs.title: Vectorized block
docs.text:
A vectorized target receives the entire active block at once and returns one fitness per row:

def sphere_block(x):                # x: (pop, ndim) -> (pop,)
    return np.sum(x**2, axis=1)

model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere_block), bounds, epochs, pop_size)

One call per epoch instead of one per individual — typically an order of magnitude faster for NumPy-shaped objectives. The contract and pitfalls are on Vectorized targets.

docs.title: How dispatch works
docs.text:
KernelBuffer.apply(x, idx) first normalizes idx into a row selection, then picks the path from that selection and the marker:

Call Path NFE apply(x, idx=one row) — int, np.intp (what pop.best returns), or a 0-d integer array target.evaluate(x); a vectorized target gets it as a (1, ndim) block and the single score is unwrapped 1 apply(x, idx=block) with target.vectorized — slice, index array, boolean mask target.evaluate_matrix(block) len(block) apply(x, idx=block), plain target np.apply_along_axis(...) over the rows 1 per row apply(x, idx) selecting no rows (empty mask, all rows removed) nothing is evaluated 0

With no index, apply writes and scores the active rows only (mask.founds), so removed individuals are never re-scored and never spend budget.

The counter charges one evaluation per individual scored, never per call and never per dimension: a NumPy row index is one individual (not ndim of them), a mask costs the rows it selects, and the whole-block form costs the active rows. The same selection therefore costs the same in both scoring modes.

docs.title: Equivalence
docs.text:
The two modes produce identical fitness — only the dispatch differs:

x = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [-3.0, 0.5], [0.0, 0.0]])

rowwise   = [sphere(row) for row in x]
block     = TargetFunction(cm.vectorized_target(sphere_block), BOUNDS)

np.testing.assert_allclose(rowwise, block.evaluate_matrix(x))

docs.title: Evaluating a single solution
docs.text:
tf.evaluate(x) is the one-individual path: it spends a single evaluation and works with both scoring modes — a vectorized target is handed a (1, ndim) block and its single score is returned as a scalar. tf.evaluate_matrix(x) is the block path and rejects a bare solution vector, so an individual can never be mis-counted as ndim evaluations:

tf.evaluate(x_row)                # 1 NFE, plain or vectorized target
tf.evaluate_matrix(x_block)       # len(x_block) NFE

docs.title: Correctness checklist for a block objective
docs.text:
• Shape in, shape out: returns exactly (len(x),) — one value per row.
  • Axis: reductions use axis=1 (per row), never the default whole-array sum.
  • dtype: float in, float out; float(...) a scalar result per row.
  • No in-place writes to x — it is the live buffer's solution block.
  • Equivalence: assert your block version against the row-wise version on a small block before trusting it at scale.

docs.title: Vectorized targets
docs.text:
Wrapping an objective with cm.vectorized_target declares that it can score a whole (pop, ndim) block in one call. KernelBuffer.apply then dispatches the entire active block through a single evaluate_matrix instead of one apply_along_axis call per individual.

import numpy as np

import cmenpy as cm


def sphere_block(x):            # x: (pop, ndim) -> (pop,)
    return np.sum(x**2, axis=1)


model = MyAlgorithm(seed=1)
best = model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere_block), bounds, epochs, pop_size)

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
• In: a 2-D array of shape (k, ndim) — the active solutions.
  • Out: a 1-D array of shape (k,) — one fitness per row, in order.
  • The block x is the live buffer's solution rows: do not modify it.
  • The result must be assignable to the fitness column — same length, numeric.

Fitness equivalence with the row-by-row form is the whole point: block(x)[i] == row(x[i]) for every row.

docs.title: How the marker is detected
docs.text:
TargetFunction checks getattr(target, "vectorized", False) is True. The identity comparison means:

  • cm.vectorized_target(f) — always works (the wrapper sets vectorized = True);
  • a class with a vectorized = True attribute and a __call__ scoring a block — also accepted;
  • a truthy stand-in (vectorized = 1, a non-empty string) — not accepted;
  • a plain function — never vectorized.

cm.vectorized_target is the supported, self-documenting way to set it. Calling evaluate_matrix on a non-vectorized target raises:

TypeError: Target is not vectorized; wrap it with `vectorized_target`.

docs.title: Pure NumPy
docs.text:
def rastrigin_block(x):
    return 10 * x.shape[1] + np.sum(x**2 - 10 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * x), axis=1)


def rosenbrock_block(x):
    return np.sum(100.0 * (x[:, 1:] - x[:, :-1] ** 2) ** 2 + (1 - x[:, :-1]) ** 2,
                  axis=1)

docs.title: Compiled block kernel
docs.text:
Combine a @cm.precompile kernel with the wrapper — the kernel scores the block in Numba, the wrapper marks it:

@cm.precompile
def sphere_block(X: "Array[float, 2]"):
    out = np.empty(X.shape[0])

    for i in range(X.shape[0]):
        acc = 0.0
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            acc += X[i, j] * X[i, j]
        out[i] = acc

    return out


model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere_block), bounds, epochs, pop_size)

Inside a @cm.template model the same kernel is a method and inherits the model's compile options.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wrong axis — np.sum(x**2) sums the whole block into a scalar; use axis=1.
  • Returning a scalar or a list — must be a (k,) array; a scalar broadcasts and corrupts the fitness column.
  • Modifying x — it is the population's own storage.
  • dtype drift — return floats; integer outputs truncate fitness.
  • Shape mismatch — returning (k, 1) or a transposed (ndim, k) fails (or silently broadcasts) when written to the fitness column.

docs.title: Not @cm.vectorize
docs.text: @cm.vectorize builds a NumPy ufunc from a scalar kernel — it maps one value to one value and cannot turn (pop, ndim) into (pop,). For block objectives use @cm.precompile (or plain NumPy) and mark the result with cm.vectorized_target.
